rules.title: California Just Cause Eviction Requirement (CIV 1946.2)
rules.requirement: After a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy. For tenancies with multiple tenants added before 24 months, just cause applies if all tenants have occupied 12+ months or one tenant has occupied 24+ months.
rules.quoted_span: after a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential real property in California where tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied for 12 months or more; for multiple tenants, just cause applies if all tenants occupied 12+ months or one tenant occupied 24+ months
rules.exemptions: Transient and tourist hotel occupancy; housing in nonprofit hospitals, religious facilities, extended care facilities, licensed residential care facilities for elderly, adult residential facilities; dormitories owned by institutions of higher education or K-12 schools; housing where tenant shares bathroom or kitchen with owner; single-family owner-occupied residences with max 2 units or bedrooms; mobilehomes; two-unit properties where owner occupied one unit as principal residence at tenancy start; housing issued certificate of occupancy within 15 years (non-mobilehome); alienable single units owned by non-REIT, non-corporate entities; affordable housing restricted by deed or regulatory agreement
rules.conflict_note: Local ordinances adopted on or before 2019-09-01, or those adopted/amended after 2019-09-01 that are more protective than this section apply instead. Local ordinances adopted after 2019-09-01 that are less protective shall not be enforced unless this section is repealed.
rules.sanctions: Material violation renders notice of termination void. Owner liable for actual damages, reasonable attorney's fees and costs at court discretion, up to three times actual damages upon showing willful or oppressive conduct/fraud/malice, and possible punitive damages. Attorney General and city/county counsel may seek injunctive relief.

rules.title: Cure Period for Curable Lease Violations (CIV 1946.2(c))
rules.requirement: Before owner issues notice to terminate for just cause based on curable lease violation, owner must first give notice of violation with opportunity to cure pursuant to CCP 1161(3). If violation not cured within specified time period, three-day notice to quit may be served thereafter.
rules.quoted_span:
Before an owner of residential real property issues a notice to terminate a tenancy for just cause that is a curable lease violation, the
owner shall first give notice of the violation to the tenant with an opportunity to cure the violation pursuant to paragraph (3) of Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure. If the violation is not cured within the time period set forth in the notice, a three-day notice to quit without an opportunity to cure may thereafter be served to terminate the tenancy.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential real property in California where tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied 12+ months and curable lease violation exists
rules.sanctions: Owner must comply with notice and cure procedure; failure to provide cure opportunity may affect validity of subsequent three-day notice

rule.title: At-Fault Just Cause Grounds (CIV 1946.2(b)(1))
rule.requirement: Owner may terminate for at-fault just cause including: default in rent payment; breach of material lease term after written notice to cure; maintaining/committing nuisance; committing waste; refusal to execute lease renewal (leases terminated 2020-01-01 or later); criminal activity on property or directed at owner; unauthorized assignment or subletting; refusal to allow owner entry; unlawful use of premises; failure to vacate after employment termination; failure to deliver possession after notice to vacate.
rule.quoted_span: At-fault just cause, which means any of the following: (A) Default in the payment of rent. (B) A breach of a material term of the lease, as described in paragraph (3) of Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure, including, but not limited to, violation of a provision of the lease after being issued a written notice to correct the violation. (C) Maintaining, committing, or permitting the maintenance or commission of a nuisance as described in paragraph (4) of Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure. (D) Committing waste as described in paragraph (4) of Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure. (E) The tenant had a written lease that terminated on or after January 1, 2020, or January 1, 2022, if the lease is for a tenancy in a mobilehome, and after a written request or demand from the owner, the tenant has refused to execute a written extension or renewal of the lease for an additional term of similar duration with similar provisions, provided that those terms do not violate this section or any other provision of law. (F) Criminal activity by the tenant on the residential real property, including any common areas, or any criminal activity or criminal threat, as defined in subdivision (a) of Section 422 of the Penal Code, on or off the residential real property, that is directed at any owner or agent of the owner of the residential real property. (G) Assigning or subletting the premises in violation of the tenant's lease, as described in paragraph (4) of Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure. (H) The tenant's refusal to allow the owner to enter the residential real property as authorized by Sections 1101.5 and 1954 of this code, and Sections 13113.7 and 17926.1 of the Health and Safety Code. (I) Using the premises for an unlawful purpose as described in paragraph (4) of Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure. (J) The employee, agent, or licensee's failure to vacate after their termination as an employee, agent, or a licensee as described in paragraph (1) of Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure. (K) When the tenant fails to deliver possession of the residential real property after providing the owner written notice as provided in Section 1946 of the tenant's intention to terminate the hiring of the real property, or makes a written offer to surrender that is accepted in writing by the owner, but fails to deliver possession at the time specified in that written notice as described in paragraph (5) of Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
rule.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential real property in California where tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied 12+ months and one or more at-fault grounds exist
rule.sanctions: Compliance required; material violation of notice renders termination void; owner attempting eviction in material violation liable for damages

rule.title: No-Fault Just Cause Grounds - Owner/Family Occupancy (CIV 1946.2(b)(2)(A))
rule.requirement: Owner may terminate for intent to occupy residential property by owner or owner's spouse, domestic partner, children, grandchildren, parents, or grandparents for minimum 12 continuous months as primary residence. For leases entered on or after 2020-07-01 (2022-07-01 for mobilehomes), this applies only if tenant agrees in writing or lease allows unilateral termination. Intended occupant must move in within 90 days after tenant vacates and occupy as primary residence for at least 12 consecutive months. If intended occupant fails to occupy within 90 days or fails 12-month continuous occupancy, owner must offer unit to vacating tenant at same rent and reimburse reasonable moving expenses.
rule.quoted_span: Intent to occupy the residential real property by the owner or the owner's spouse, domestic partner, children, grandchildren, parents, or grandparents for a minimum of 12 continuous months as that person's primary residence. For leases entered into on or after July 1, 2020, or July 1, 2022, if the lease is for a tenancy in a mobilehome, clause (i) shall apply only if the tenant agrees, in writing, to the termination, or if a provision of the lease allows the owner to terminate the lease if the owner, or the owner's spouse, domestic partner, children, grandchildren, parents, or grandparents, unilaterally decides to occupy the residential real property. Clause (i) applies only if the intended occupant moves into the rental unit within 90 days after the tenant vacates and occupies the rental unit as a primary residence for at least 12 consecutive months. If the intended occupant fails to occupy the rental unit within 90 days after the tenant vacates or fails to occupy the rental unit as their primary residence for at least 12 consecutive months, the owner shall offer the unit to the tenant who vacated it at the same rent and lease terms in effect at the time the tenant vacated and shall reimburse the tenant for reasonable moving expenses incurred in excess of any relocation assistance that was paid to the tenant in connection with the written notice.
rule.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential real property in California where tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied 12+ months and owner or specified family member intends to occupy as primary residence for 12+ continuous months, with 90-day move-in and 12-month occupancy requirements
rule.exemptions: Does not apply if intended occupant already occupies rental unit on property or similar vacancy exists; for leases entered on/after 2020-07-01 (2022-07-01 mobilehomes), requires tenant written agreement or unilateral lease termination provision
rule.conflict_note: 90-day move-in requirement and 12-month occupancy requirement are conditions precedent; failure to comply triggers obligation to re-offer unit to prior tenant at same rent with moving expense reimbursement
rule.sanctions: If intended occupant fails to occupy within 90 days or fails 12-month occupancy requirement, owner must offer unit to prior tenant at same rent and lease terms and reimburse reasonable moving expenses exceeding any relocation assistance already paid

rule.title: No-Fault Just Cause Grounds - Government Habitability/Vacancy Orders (CIV 1946.2(b)(2)(C))
rule.requirement: Owner may terminate for no-fault just cause when complying with government agency or court orders relating to habitability requiring vacation, general vacation orders, or local ordinances necessitating vacation. If tenant is at fault for condition triggering order, tenant not entitled to relocation assistance.
rule.quoted_span: The owner complying with any of the following: (I) An order issued by a government agency or court relating to habitability that necessitates vacating the residential real property. (II) An order issued by a government agency or court to vacate the residential real property. (III) A local ordinance that necessitates vacating the residential real property. If it is determined by any government agency or court that the tenant is at fault for the condition or conditions triggering the order or need to vacate under clause (i), the tenant shall not be entitled to relocation assistance as outlined in paragraph (3) of subdivision (d).
rule.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential real property in California where tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied 12+ months and owner is complying with government agency/court order or local ordinance requiring vacancy
rule.exemptions: Relocation assistance not required if tenant is at fault for condition triggering order
rule.sanctions: Termination for non-fault cause requires relocation assistance (one month rent or final month waiver) unless tenant at fault; relocation assistance provided within 15 days

rule.title: No-Fault Just Cause Grounds - Demolition or Substantial Remodel (CIV 1946.2(b)(2)(D))
rule.requirement: Owner may terminate for no-fault just cause based on intent to demolish or substantially remodel residential property. Substantial remodel means replacement or substantial modification of structural, electrical, plumbing, or mechanical systems requiring permit, or abatement of hazardous materials (lead, mold, asbestos), that cannot be reasonably accomplished with tenant remaining and requires 30+ consecutive day vacation. Cosmetic improvements alone do not qualify. Owner notice must state intent, description of remodel with timeline or demolition date, copy of permit or signed contractor agreement, and inform tenant of right to reoccupy following remodel. Tenant not required to vacate days when safe occupancy maintained under health/safety codes. If remodel not commenced or completed, owner must offer unit to vacating tenant at same rent.
rule.quoted_span: Intent to demolish or to substantially remodel the residential real property. For purposes of this subparagraph, 'substantially remodel' means either of the following that cannot be reasonably accomplished in a safe manner that allows the tenant to remain living in the place and that requires the tenant to vacate the residential real property for at least 30 consecutive days: (I) The replacement or substantial modification of any structural, electrical, plumbing, or mechanical system that requires a permit from a governmental agency. (II) The abatement of hazardous materials, including lead-based paint, mold, or asbestos, in accordance with applicable federal, state, and local laws. For purposes of this subparagraph, a tenant is not required to vacate the residential real property on any days where a tenant could continue living in the residential real property without violating health, safety, and habitability codes and laws. Cosmetic improvements alone, including painting, decorating, and minor repairs, or other work that can be performed safely without having the residential real property vacated, do not qualify as substantial remodel.
rule.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential real property in California where tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied 12+ months and owner intends to demolish or substantially remodel, requiring 30+ consecutive day vacation and involving structural/mechanical work with permit or hazardous materials abatement that cannot be safely accomplished with tenant present
rule.exemptions: Does not apply to cosmetic improvements (painting, decorating, minor repairs) or work safely performable without vacation; tenant not required to vacate days when safe occupancy maintained under health/safety codes
rule.conflict_note: If remodel not commenced or completed, owner must offer unit to vacating tenant at same rent and lease terms; tenant may request proof of intended occupant for owner-occupancy terminations within 30 days
rule.sanctions: Termination for no-fault cause requires relocation assistance (one month rent or final month waiver) within 15 days; if remodel not completed, must re-offer at same rent; material violation renders notice void

rule.title: Relocation Assistance for No-Fault Terminations (CIV 1946.2(d))
rule.requirement: For no-fault just cause terminations, owner must at option either: (1) provide direct payment relocation assistance to tenant, or (2) waive in writing final month rent prior to rent becoming due. Amount equals one month of tenant's rent in effect when notice issued. Relocation assistance must be provided within 15 calendar days of notice service. If tenant fails to vacate after expiration, relocation assistance becomes recoverable as damages. Relocation assistance/rent waiver required by this section credited against other relocation assistance required by law. Owner's failure to strictly comply renders notice void.
rule.quoted_span: For a tenancy for which just cause is required to terminate the tenancy under subdivision (a), if an owner of residential real property issues a termination notice based on a no-fault just cause described in paragraph (2) of subdivision (b), the owner shall, regardless of the tenant's income, at the owner's option, do one of the following: (A) Assist the tenant to relocate by providing a direct payment to the tenant as described in paragraph (3). (B) Waive in writing the payment of rent for the final month of the tenancy, prior to the rent becoming due. The amount of relocation assistance or rent waiver shall be equal to one month of the tenant's rent that was in effect when the owner issued the notice to terminate the tenancy. Any relocation assistance shall be provided within 15 calendar days of service of the notice.
rule.coverage_conditions: Applies to all no-fault just cause terminations under CIV 1946.2(b)(2) for residential real property where tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied 12+ months
rule.conflict_note: Relocation assistance/rent waiver required by this section credited against other relocation assistance required by law; owner may choose between direct payment or rent waiver; failure to strictly comply renders notice void
rule.sanctions: Strict compliance required; failure renders termination notice void; if tenant fails to vacate after expiration, relocation assistance amount becomes recoverable as damages in possession action

rule.title: Owner Notice Requirements to Tenant (CIV 1946.2(f))
rule.requirement: Owner must provide notice to tenant about just cause requirement. For tenancies commenced or renewed on/after 2020-07-01 (2022-07-01 for mobilehomes), notice must be in lease/rental agreement, as addendum, or as signed written notice with copy to tenant. For pre-existing tenancies, notice required by 2020-08-01 (2022-08-01 for mobilehomes) or as addendum. Notice minimum 12-point type, informing tenant that California law limits rent increases (CIV 1947.12) and requires landlord to state cause for termination after 12 months continuous occupation (CIV 1946.2).
rule.quoted_span: An owner of residential real property subject to this section shall provide notice to the tenant as follows: (1)(A) Except as provided in subparagraph (B), for any tenancy commenced or renewed on or after July 1, 2020, in the lease or rental agreement, as an addendum to the lease or rental agreement, or as a written notice signed by the tenant, with a copy provided to the tenant. (2)(A) Except as provided in subparagraph (B), for a tenancy existing prior to July 1, 2020, by written notice to the tenant no later than August 1, 2020, or as an addendum to the lease or rental agreement. (3) The notification or lease provision shall be in no less than 12-point type, and shall include the following: 'California law limits the amount your rent can be increased. See Section 1947.12 of the Civil Code for more information. California law also provides that after all of the tenants have continuously and lawfully occupied the property for 12 months or more or at least one of the tenants has continuously and lawfully occupied the property for 24 months or more, a landlord must provide a statement of cause in any notice to terminate a tenancy. See Section 1946.2 of the Civil Code for more information.'
rule.coverage_conditions: Applies to all residential real property subject to CIV 1946.2 in California
rule.conflict_note: Different timing requirements for new vs. pre-existing tenancies; mobilehomes have different deadlines (2022-07-01 for new, 2022-08-01 for existing)
rule.sanctions: Owner's failure to comply with notice requirements renders termination notice void

rule.title: Local Ordinance Preemption and Interaction (CIV 1946.2(i))
rule.requirement: State law does not apply to residential real property subject to local ordinance adopted on/before 2019-09-01 requiring just cause for termination; local ordinance applies instead. State law does not apply to property subject to local ordinance adopted/amended after 2019-09-01 that is more protective than state law (limiting termination reasons further, providing higher relocation assistance, or additional tenant protections, with local binding finding that ordinance more protective). Property not subject to both local ordinance and state law. Local ordinance adopted after 2019-09-01 less protective than state law shall not be enforced unless state law repealed.
rule.quoted_span: This section does not apply to the following residential real property: (A) Residential real property subject to a local ordinance requiring just cause for termination of a residential tenancy adopted on or before September 1, 2019, in which case the local ordinance shall apply. (B) Residential real property subject to a local ordinance requiring just cause for termination of a residential tenancy adopted or amended after September 1, 2019, that is more protective than this section, in which case the local ordinance shall apply. For purposes of this subparagraph, an ordinance is 'more protective' if it meets all of the following criteria: (i) The just cause for termination of a residential tenancy under the local ordinance is consistent with this section. (ii) The ordinance further limits the reasons for termination of a residential tenancy, provides for higher relocation assistance amounts, or provides additional tenant protections that are not prohibited by any other provision of law. (iii) The local government has made a binding finding within their local ordinance that the ordinance is more protective than the provisions of this section. A residential real property shall not be subject to both a local ordinance requiring just cause for termination of a residential tenancy and this section. A local ordinance adopted after September 1, 2019, that is less protective than this section shall not be enforced unless this section is repealed.
rule.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential real property in California; outcome depends on existence and date of local just cause ordinance and comparative protectiveness
rule.exemptions: Local ordinances adopted on/before 2019-09-01; local ordinances adopted/amended after 2019-09-01 that are more protective (with local binding finding) apply instead of state law
rule.conflict_note: Properties subject to pre-2019-09-01 local ordinance or more protective post-2019-09-01 local ordinance exempt from state law; less protective post-2019-09-01 ordinances preempted unless state law repealed; property cannot be subject to both state and local ordinance
rule.sanctions: Property must be subject to either state law or qualifying local ordinance, not both; enforcement of less protective local ordinances prohibited unless state law repealed

rule.title: Enforcement and Remedies for Material Violations (CIV 1946.2(h))
rule.requirement: Owner attempting to recover possession in material violation liable to tenant for: actual damages; reasonable attorney's fees and costs at court discretion; up to three times actual damages upon showing willful or oppressive conduct, fraud, or malice; and possible punitive damages. Attorney General or city/county counsel may seek injunctive relief for violations. Failure to strictly comply with relocation assistance requirement or notice requirements renders termination notice void.
rule.quoted_span: An owner who attempts to recover possession of a rental unit in material violation of this section shall be liable to the tenant in a civil action for all of the following: (A) Actual damages. (B) In the court's discretion, reasonable attorney's fees and costs. (C) Upon a showing that the owner has acted willfully or with oppression, fraud, or malice, up to three times the actual damages. An award may also be entered for punitive damages for the benefit of the tenant against the owner. The Attorney General, in the name of the people of the State of California, and the city attorney or county counsel in the jurisdiction in which the rental unit is located, in the name of the city or county, may seek injunctive relief based on violations of this section.
rule.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential real property in California where owner attempts to recover possession in material violation of CIV 1946.2
rule.conflict_note: Material violation includes failure to provide just cause, failure to comply with notice requirements, and failure to strictly comply with relocation assistance requirements
rule.sanctions: Liable for actual damages, reasonable attorney's fees/costs at discretion, up to treble damages if willful/oppressive/fraud/malice, possible punitive damages; Attorney General, city attorney, or county counsel may seek injunctive relief; material violation renders termination notice void
